q: A client insists a 5% Turnitin score means their document is fine. How do you respond?
a: I explain that similarity is not plagiarism: the tool matches strings, so an uncited paraphrase scores zero yet is still plagiarism, and a properly quoted literature review can score 25% and be fine. I then offer the check that actually matters: a citation-to-reference audit where every in-text citation is matched to a list entry and every entry back to the text. On a recent 88-entry list that audit found 8 orphan citations that Turnitin could never have flagged. That reframes the job from "lower a number" to "make the references defensible".

q: What is the difference between a citation and a reference?
a: A citation is the in-text marker, either `(Author, Year)` in author-date styles or a number like `[4]` in numeric styles; it is short and repeated. A reference is the full entry in the list at the end, appearing once per source, with author, date, title, source and locator such as a DOI. Reference managers keep the two linked so that changing the style rewrites both. In Word you can see the link because a plugin citation is a field code, not plain text.

q: When does paraphrasing still count as plagiarism?
a: When the structure and sequence of ideas are copied with only word substitutions, which is called patchwriting, or when the paraphrase carries no citation at all. A genuine paraphrase restates the idea in your own sentence structure and still credits the author. My rule for clients is that a paraphrase should be written after closing the source, then checked against it for accuracy, then cited.

chapter: Anatomy of a reference (author, year, title, source, DOI)
q: Why do reference managers store references as fields rather than formatted text?
a: Because a style is a transformation applied to fields, not a property of the data. With author, year, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI in separate fields, EndNote or Zotero can render the same record as APA, Vancouver or IEEE in a second. A pasted formatted string cannot be re-rendered without parsing it back into fields, which is unreliable. When a client sends a hand-typed list, my first step is always to rebuild it as fielded records, usually by DOI lookup, precisely so the style can change later.

chapter: Anatomy of a reference (author, year, title, source, DOI)
q: A reference has both a DOI and a URL. Which do you keep?
a: The DOI, in link form. A DOI is persistent and resolves through doi.org regardless of publisher website changes, while a URL breaks when the site is reorganised. APA 7, MLA 9 and Chicago all prefer the DOI. I keep the URL only when there is no DOI, and I add a retrieval date only when the page content is designed to change, such as a live dashboard or a wiki.

chapter: Anatomy of a reference (author, year, title, source, DOI)
q: How do you handle a source with no date?
a: In APA and Harvard I write `n.d.` in the date position, both in text `(Raza, n.d.)` and in the list. In Chicago it is `n.d.` in author-date and `[n.d.]` in a bibliography. In MLA the date is simply omitted and an access date is added. I also try to find a date first: page footers, the HTML `<meta>` tags, and the Wayback Machine often reveal one, and a real date is always better than `n.d.`.

q: What are the key differences between APA 6 and APA 7 that you check for when updating a document?
a: Four things first: "et al." now applies from the first citation for three or more authors, up to 20 authors appear in the list instead of seven, DOIs are formatted as https://doi.org/ links with no "doi:" or "Retrieved from", and the publisher location is dropped from book references. I also check for a running head on student papers, which APA 7 removed. In EndNote or Zotero the conversion is just switching the output style to APA 7th, but hand-typed lists must be rebuilt, and I quote the job accordingly.

q: How do you handle a corporate author such as a title-insurance underwriter in APA?
a: The organisation is the author: `Stewart Title Guaranty Company. (2021). Rate manual for Texas. https://...`. In text I introduce an abbreviation on first use, `(Stewart Title Guaranty Company [STGC], 2021)`, and use `(STGC, 2021)` afterwards. If the author and publisher are the same organisation, APA 7 omits the publisher element to avoid repetition. In the reference list it sorts by the first significant word of the organisation's name.

q: A client's reference list mixes sentence case and title case. Does it matter?
a: Yes, because APA prescribes sentence case for article and book titles and title case for journal names, so a mixed list reads as careless to a marker. In practice I fix it in the reference manager, not in Word: EndNote has a "Change Case" edit and Zotero has "Transform Text → Sentence case" on the title field, and I preserve proper nouns manually afterwards. Fixing the source records means the next export is right too.

q: A publisher's handbook needs Chicago notes-bibliography. What is your Word workflow?
a: I insert every citation as a footnote through the reference manager's plugin rather than by hand, so numbering stays automatic when the editor moves paragraphs. In Zotero that means setting Document Preferences to "Footnotes" with the Chicago 17th note style; in EndNote it means inserting the citation inside a Word footnote created with Ctrl+Alt+F. The plugin then handles full-versus-short notes automatically and builds the bibliography. On a recent 767-page handbook that automation was the difference between a two-day job and a two-week one.

q: Why does MLA omit the year from in-text citations?
a: Because MLA grew out of literary scholarship where the page of the quoted passage matters far more than the publication date, and readers locate the full details in Works Cited by author name. It keeps the sentence uncluttered, `(Raza 14)`. The trade-off is that two works by one author must be distinguished by a short title in the citation, which is slightly clumsier than APA's 2023a/2023b convention.

q: What is the difference between a footnote and a bibliography entry in Chicago?
a: A note is a sentence-like reference tied to a specific place in the text: author's name in natural order, elements separated by commas, publication details in brackets, and a page number for that citation. A bibliography entry is a list record: surname first for sorting, elements separated by full stops, no page for books and a full range for articles. The bibliography is optional if notes are complete, but most clients want both, and the manager generates the second from the first.

q: How do you verify that every citation has a reference and vice versa in a long document?
a: If the citations were inserted by a plugin, the tool does it: EndNote's Convert to Unformatted Citations shows the raw keys, and its travelling library is exactly the set of cited records; Zotero's "Refresh" rebuilds the bibliography from the citations only, so anything uncited disappears. If the citations are plain text, I extract them with a wildcard search or a short Python regex, build a set of author-year keys, and compare against the list keys. For an 88-entry dissertation I found 8 orphan citations and 25 uncited entries that way, and sent the client a table rather than a vague "some references are missing".

q: Why are numeric styles harder to maintain manually than author-date styles?
a: Because the key is positional. Inserting one new citation early in the text shifts every subsequent number, and every repeated citation must be updated too. Author-date keys are stable: `(Raza, 2023)` means the same thing wherever it appears. So for IEEE or Vancouver I refuse to work in plain text and always rebuild the citations as plugin fields, then let "Update Citations and Bibliography" do the renumbering.

q: A client wants to include works they read but did not cite. What do you tell them?
a: It depends on the style. Chicago allows a bibliography of works consulted, and some universities allow a separate "Bibliography" after "References". APA and MLA do not: the list must contain only cited works. My usual compromise is two lists, "References" for cited works and "Further reading" for the rest, if the department accepts it, and I ask the client to confirm with their supervisor before I format either.

chapter: EndNote: creating a library, importing (PubMed, Google Scholar, PDF), groups
q: A client sends you an EndNote library and half the references show no PDF. What happened and what do you do?
a: Almost always they sent the `.enl` without the `.Data` folder, or they zipped the folder but the PDFs were linked as absolute paths on their machine rather than copied into the library. I ask for a compressed library (`File → Compressed Library`, which creates an `.enlx` with attachments), or the `.Data` folder. If the PDFs are genuinely missing, I run Find Full Text against the records with DOIs, which typically recovers open-access copies for a third to half of a medical list. I then report which records still need the client to supply the file.

chapter: EndNote: creating a library, importing (PubMed, Google Scholar, PDF), groups
q: Why is importing better than typing references, and when do you still type?
a: Importing from PubMed, Crossref or a PDF's embedded DOI gives fielded, publisher-verified metadata with the DOI, which removes the two commonest errors in hand-typed lists: wrong page ranges and missing DOIs. Typing is for sources with no digital record, such as a client's internal SOP, a personal communication or an unpublished report. Even then I choose the correct Reference Type first so the output style knows how to render it, and I fill Author as `Surname, First` per line so EndNote parses names correctly.

chapter: EndNote: creating a library, importing (PubMed, Google Scholar, PDF), groups
q: How would you organise a 400-reference library for a multi-chapter handbook?
a: One group set for the project, one custom group per chapter so the chapter authors see only their sources, and two smart groups for QA: "No DOI" and "Journal articles with empty pages". I also keep an "Unfiled" habit: any reference not yet in a chapter group is triaged weekly. Groups do not duplicate records, so a source cited in three chapters lives once and is edited once, which is the whole point of a manager over a per-chapter Word list.

chapter: EndNote Cite While You Write in Word
q: A co-author without EndNote opens the document and the bibliography is fine, but they cannot add citations. Why?
a: The bibliography is stored text inside field codes and the travelling library is embedded, so the document renders correctly anywhere. Adding a citation needs the CWYW add-in and a library. My practical answer is either they install EndNote and use Export Travelling Library to get the cited records, or they add citations in unformatted form by typing `{Surname, Year #RecordNumber}` where the record number matches my library, and I format the document at the end. The second route works well for busy co-authors.

chapter: EndNote Cite While You Write in Word
q: How do you switch a formatted document from APA 7 to Vancouver?
a: Pick Vancouver in the Style dropdown on the EndNote tab and click Update Citations and Bibliography. Every `(Raza, 2023)` becomes a number in order of first appearance and the bibliography is renumbered and re-sorted. What I check afterwards is manual text that assumed author-date, such as "Raza (2023) found", which becomes "Raza (1) found" and needs rewording, and any citation where I had excluded the author. The switch is seconds; the read-through of narrative sentences is the real work.

chapter: EndNote Cite While You Write in Word
q: What breaks CWYW documents in practice?
a: Three things. Track Changes turned on during updates, which produces enormous tracked rewrites of the bibliography. Copying citations between documents whose libraries have different record numbers, so `#412` points at the wrong record; the fix is Convert to Unformatted first and let EndNote match on author-year-title from the travelling library. And saving as `.doc` or opening in Google Docs, which can strip or flatten field codes. I keep a formatted copy and a plain-text copy (Convert to Plain Text) at each milestone so that nothing is ever lost.

chapter: Mendeley: Reference Manager, web importer, Mendeley Cite
q: A client wrote their thesis with the old Mendeley Desktop plugin. What are their options now?
a: Mendeley Cite cannot edit citations inserted by the retired MS Word plugin, so the choices are to keep the document as is and finish with plain text, or to migrate. Migration means exporting the old library to BibTeX or RIS, importing into Reference Manager, and re-inserting each citation with Cite while carrying over page numbers. On a 120-citation thesis that is roughly a day, so I quote it as a separate line item and explain that the alternative, editing text by hand, will drift out of sync with the list. Alternatively Zotero imports the same BibTeX and its Word plugin can rebuild the document just as well.

chapter: Mendeley: Reference Manager, web importer, Mendeley Cite
q: Compare Mendeley Cite with EndNote's Cite While You Write.
a: Both insert live citations and a bibliography and both embed the cited data in the document. CWYW is a COM add-in, Windows and Mac only, fast in very long documents once Instant Formatting is off, and it has a full style editor. Mendeley Cite is an Office add-in that runs in Word Online and on iPad, needs no desktop app, and uses CSL styles from the shared repository, but it has no built-in style editor and handles footnote styles less smoothly. For a medical thesis in a university with EndNote licences I use CWYW; for a distributed team on Microsoft 365 with no budget, Mendeley Cite or Zotero.

chapter: Mendeley: Reference Manager, web importer, Mendeley Cite
q: How does Mendeley extract metadata from a dropped PDF, and when does it fail?
a: It reads the PDF's embedded metadata and first-page text, looks for a DOI, and queries Crossref to fill the record; if there is no DOI it guesses title and authors from the largest text on page one. It fails on scanned PDFs without a text layer, on preprints and reports with no DOI, and on PDFs whose first page is a cover sheet from a database. For those I use Add new → Identifier with the DOI or PMID if I can find it, or fill the fields manually after choosing the correct reference type.

chapter: Zotero as the free alternative & Zotero Connector
q: Why might you recommend Zotero over EndNote to a small consultancy producing policy manuals?
a: Cost and openness. Zotero is free for unlimited references, group libraries have no member limit, and its data lives in open formats (CSL-JSON, BibTeX, RIS) so nothing is locked to a vendor. The Word plugin does everything the consultancy needs, including footnote styles for Chicago-formatted manuals and one-click style switching, and the Connector captures government reports and web pages better than EndNote does. The trade-offs are 300 MB of free attachment storage, so PDFs need a paid plan or linked files, and the absence of a built-in style editor, which matters only if the house style is unusual.

chapter: Zotero as the free alternative & Zotero Connector
q: How does Zotero embed cited data in a Word document, and why does it matter?
a: Each citation is a Word field whose code contains CSL-JSON for the cited items. That means a collaborator with Zotero but without my library can still refresh the bibliography, and the document is recoverable if my library is lost. It also means the document is large and fragile if someone edits the field code by hand or opens it in an editor that strips fields. So I keep Fields mode for editing and deliver an unlinked copy for print.

chapter: Zotero as the free alternative & Zotero Connector
q: What is the difference between a collection, a tag and a saved search in Zotero?
a: A collection is a manual folder-like container that an item can belong to many times over; deleting an item from a collection does not delete it. A tag is a label attached to the item itself, useful for status such as "to-read" or "checked", and colour-coded tags can be toggled with number keys. A saved search is a dynamic query that lists matching items live, so it is the tool for QA lists like "journal articles with no DOI". I use collections per chapter, tags for workflow state, and saved searches for quality checks.

q: A client says their Zotero highlights disappeared after they sent the PDF to a colleague. What happened?
a: Zotero stores annotations in its own database, not in the PDF, so the file in the storage folder is the clean original. The colleague opened an unannotated PDF. The fix is to export via right-click → Export PDF, which writes a copy with the annotations embedded, or to share through a group library where the annotations sync as items. I explain the design reason too: keeping annotations separate lets Zotero keep them even if the PDF is replaced by a better copy.

q: How do you turn a folder of 300 unnamed PDFs into a usable reference library, and what does not automate?
a: Bulk-import the folder, run metadata retrieval on all items, and sort by title to isolate the failures. Files with an embedded DOI match through Crossref; the failures are scans, cover-sheeted database downloads and grey literature. For those I read the first page, look up DOIs or PMIDs by title in Crossref or PubMed and use the identifier tool, and I enter the rest manually with the right item type. Then I rename every file from metadata so the PDF names match the citations. On a recent job that was 80 percent automated in an hour and 20 percent manual over an afternoon.

q: Stored attachments or linked files for a team?
a: Stored, unless the team already has a shared file server they trust. Stored files sync with the library, survive folder moves and are included in compressed or RDF exports. Linked files save cloud storage and are fine for one person on one machine, but the moment a second person opens the library the links point at paths that do not exist for them. For Zotero groups with a storage cap, I set up WebDAV or a paid plan rather than fall back to linking.

q: A university's Harvard variant differs from every built-in style. How do you deliver it?
a: I ask for the university's guide with examples for each source type, then search the Zotero Style Repository by example to find the nearest of the roughly 30 Harvard variants, often "Cite Them Right" or a specific university's own style. I fork it in the Visual CSL Editor, rename the title and id, and adjust the differences, which are usually the year in brackets, "and" versus "&", and whether the URL carries an accessed date. I test against ten fixture records and deliver the `.csl` with installation instructions for both Zotero and Mendeley Cite, so the client is not tied to my copy.

q: Why do sentence-case titles cause trouble in CSL and how do you handle them?
a: CSL can lowercase a title with `text-case="sentence"`, but it cannot know which words are proper nouns, so "Automating Rate Matrices In Texas" would become "Automating rate matrices in texas". Zotero's policy is therefore to store titles in sentence case and let styles apply title case when needed, because uppercasing is safe and lowercasing is not. So on import I run "Transform Text → Sentence case" on the title field and restore proper nouns by hand. That one-time clean-up makes every style render correctly.

q: What are the practical differences between EndNote `.ens` styles and CSL?
a: EndNote styles are edited in a form-based editor with per-type templates and a rich set of special characters, and they support features like "Title Capitalization" per style; they are proprietary and only EndNote reads them. CSL is plain XML, versioned in a public GitHub repository, shared by Zotero, Mendeley, Pandoc and many web tools, and edited in the online Visual Editor. CSL is the better long-term investment because a style written once works everywhere; the EndNote editor is quicker for a one-off tweak in a client who already runs EndNote.

q: A client is moving from EndNote to Zotero and wants PDFs and notes kept. What is the route?
a: Export from EndNote as XML, not RIS, because XML carries the notes and the full field set. Before importing, copy the library's `.Data/PDF` folder to sit next to the XML file so the relative attachment paths in the XML resolve; Zotero's importer then attaches the PDFs. After import I check reference types (EndNote "Generic" becomes Zotero "Document" and needs fixing), run Duplicate Items, and re-check a sample of 20 records field by field. Groups do not transfer, so I recreate collections from a list the client gives me.

q: What is the difference between BibTeX and BibLaTeX and when does it matter?
a: BibTeX is the 1980s format with a fixed field set and entry types like `@article` and `@misc`; BibLaTeX extends it with `@online`, `@report`, `journaltitle`, `date` with full ISO dates, `doi`, `url` and `urldate`. It matters when the client's LaTeX template loads `biblatex` with `biber`, because a classic BibTeX file with `year` and `journal` still works but loses precision, and `@online` entries are impossible in classic form. Zotero exports either, and Better BibTeX lets you pick the dialect per export.

q: Why do you convert via text formats rather than copying formatted references?
a: Because a formatted reference is a rendering, not data. Parsing "Raza, A. (2023). Title. Journal, 8(3), 210–225." back into fields is unreliable: titles with colons, corporate authors and page ranges all confuse parsers. RIS and BibTeX carry the fields explicitly, so an import is exact. If all I have is formatted text, I use the DOIs to fetch records and only parse by hand for the few sources without identifiers, and I tell the client which ones those were.

q: Describe your deduplication process for a merged library of 400 references.
a: First a full backup. Then the tool's duplicate finder with default criteria, resolving pairs by keeping the record with the DOI and the most complete fields, and merging attachments. Then a second pass with stricter criteria in EndNote (DOI added, spacing ignored) or a manual title sort in Zotero to catch variants the fuzzy match missed, such as titles with and without a subtitle. I deliberately keep preprint-versus-published pairs apart. Finally I re-run the finder to confirm zero candidates and report the numbers: 412 in, 41 duplicates merged, 371 out.

q: What metadata problems most often cause a reference list to fail review?
a: Titles in the wrong case, missing DOIs, page ranges written as `210-25`, journal names inconsistently abbreviated, and corporate authors parsed as people so that "Company, Stewart Title Guaranty" appears. All five are fixable in the library rather than the document, and I fix them there so every future render is right. I use smart groups or saved searches as a to-do list, for example "Journal Article and DOI empty", and I use Find Reference Updates or Update from DOI to pull publisher values instead of typing.

q: When would you not merge two records that look like duplicates?
a: When they are different editions of a book, a preprint and its published version, a conference paper and the journal extension, or translations. Each has its own date, pages and often its own DOI, and a reader following the citation needs the exact version. In those cases I keep both, make the titles distinguishable, and check that the text cites the correct one. A duplicate finder cannot know this, which is why merging is never fully automatic.

chapter: Footnotes, endnotes & bibliographies natively in Word (References tab)
q: When would you use Word's built-in citation tool instead of a reference manager?
a: For a short document with under about 30 sources, where the client will keep editing it without any add-in installed and the required style is one Word has, such as IEEE or Chicago. It is also what I use for client templates that must work on any machine. I avoid it for APA 7, for anything numeric with hundreds of citations, and for any project where sources are imported rather than typed, because it has no import from DOI or PubMed and its APA is still the 6th edition.

chapter: Footnotes, endnotes & bibliographies natively in Word (References tab)
q: Explain how Word numbers footnotes and what breaks the numbering.
a: Footnote references are auto-numbered fields tied to the footnote story, so inserting or deleting a note renumbers the rest instantly, and the dialog controls whether numbering is continuous, per section or per page. It breaks when someone types a superscript number manually, when a section break is missing so "restart each section" has no effect, and when a document is assembled from files with different note settings. My check on a received manuscript is to press Ctrl+Alt+F in the last paragraph: if the new note's number is not the count of existing notes plus one, some notes are fake.

chapter: Footnotes, endnotes & bibliographies natively in Word (References tab)
q: A client wants a "Bibliography" of consulted works after the "References" list produced by Zotero. How do you build it?
a: Zotero only generates cited items, so the second list is built separately. I select the consulted items in Zotero and use right-click → Create Bibliography from Items → Output Mode Bibliography → Copy to Clipboard, in the same style, and paste under a Heading 1 "Bibliography" with the same paragraph style as the References list. It is static, so I note in the hand-off that it will not update automatically and I supply the Zotero collection used to generate it so it can be regenerated.

q: A client says "use Harvard" with no further detail. What do you do before formatting?
a: I ask for the institution's referencing guide or a link to it, because Harvard variants differ on the brackets around the year, "and" versus "&", the "pp." prefix and how DOIs and accessed dates appear. If there is no guide, I propose Cite Them Right Harvard in writing and ask them to confirm; that gives me an authoritative reference for any later dispute. Then I pick the matching CSL or EndNote style, render five sample references of different types and send them for approval before doing the full list.

q: Why do numeric styles like IEEE and Vancouver order the list by citation rather than alphabetically?
a: Because the number is the link: a reader seeing [4] in the text should find [4] as the fourth entry without scanning. It also keeps the citation short in dense technical text where dozens of sources appear in one paragraph. The cost is fragility during editing, which plugins solve by renumbering on refresh, and slightly harder scanning for a reader who wants all works by one author.

q: What distinguishes Vancouver from IEEE, given both are numeric?
a: Author form (Raza A versus A. Raza), article titles (plain versus quoted), journal titles (NLM abbreviation without italics versus IEEE abbreviation with italics), the date position (after the journal in Vancouver, at the end in IEEE), page elision (210-25 versus 210–225), and the citation marker (superscript or brackets allowed in Vancouver, square brackets only in IEEE). Both list six authors before et al. I keep a one-page cheat sheet of these because journals in engineering medicine, such as biomedical engineering, sometimes ask for a hybrid.

chapter: Formatting a 767-page handbook's references & long-document workflows
q: Walk me through how you handled references in the largest document you have formatted.
a: A 767-page handbook with 25 chapters and roughly 400 references. Chapters lived as separate files during authoring, each with plugin-inserted citations, and I merged them into one document with section breaks per chapter for the final pass. I turned instant formatting off, cleaned the library first (duplicates, DOIs, sentence-case titles), ran one refresh, and then read every narrative citation. At each milestone I saved a fields copy, an unlinked plain copy and a library export. The final refresh took about three minutes; the data cleaning and the read-through were the real days of work.

chapter: Formatting a 767-page handbook's references & long-document workflows
q: How do you produce per-chapter reference lists?
a: It has to be decided before any citation goes in. In EndNote, the output style's Sections setting can create a bibliography per section, with a section break per chapter. Zotero cannot do multiple bibliographies in one file, so the honest answer is to keep chapter files separate through delivery or to build one combined list. With Word's native tool it is impossible. If the client changes their mind late, I quote a rebuild, not a tweak.

chapter: Formatting a 767-page handbook's references & long-document workflows
q: What would you never do with a long Word document that has live citations?
a: Open it in Google Docs or Pages and save, because they flatten fields; run refreshes with Track Changes on, because the tracked rewrite of the bibliography can double the file size and confuse reviewers; and use Word's Master Document feature. I also never send the fields copy to a typesetter, since their tools may not handle fields, and never name a file "final" because there is always a version after it.

chapter: Field codes behind citations (and unlinking/converting to plain text)
q: A journal rejected the submission because "the file contains field codes". What do you do?
a: Make a Save-As copy and remove the citation fields only, keeping cross-references and the TOC live if the journal wants them. For EndNote that is Convert to Plain Text, for Zotero Unlink Citations, for Mendeley Cite Export without fields, and for mixed documents a short VBA loop over add-in fields including the footnote story. Then I search the copy for `ADDIN`, `CSL_CITATION` and `EN.CITE` to prove zero remain, and I keep the fielded original for the revision round, because the journal will ask for changes and I do not want to rebuild citations from text.

chapter: Field codes behind citations (and unlinking/converting to plain text)
q: Explain what is inside a Zotero citation field and why it matters for collaboration.
a: The field code is `ADDIN ZOTERO_ITEM CSL_CITATION` followed by JSON: a citation id, properties such as the formatted text, and `citationItems` each with the item's URI and a full `itemData` block in CSL-JSON. Because the item data is embedded, any collaborator with Zotero can refresh the bibliography without owning the item; Zotero also uses the URIs to re-link items from a group library so everyone edits the same record. The trade-off is that a hand edit to the field JSON breaks the citation, and that the document is heavier than plain text.

chapter: Field codes behind citations (and unlinking/converting to plain text)
q: How would you recover citations if the client only has a PDF of the thesis?
a: Citations cannot be recovered as fields; they must be rebuilt. I extract the reference list text from the PDF, pull DOIs and PMIDs with a regex, and rebuild the library by identifier, entering the few sources without identifiers manually. Then I re-insert citations in the Word file from the PDF text by searching each author-year pattern and inserting the corresponding record, which for a plugin like Zotero is a few seconds per citation. For a 150-citation thesis that is a day, and the client gets a proper linked document out of it rather than another static text.

chapter: Collaborative libraries & version control of references
q: How do you keep three authors' citations consistent across a multi-chapter handbook?
a: One shared library that everyone cites from, a single owner responsible for cleaning and deduplication, status tags so the team can see what is verified, and an exported BibTeX copy committed to Git so every change is attributable and reviewable. In Zotero that is a group library with Better BibTeX auto-export; in EndNote it is a shared library over EndNote Online with XML exports at milestones. The rule that prevents most problems is "add by identifier, cite from the group", because hand-typed private copies are where duplicates and inconsistencies come from.

chapter: Collaborative libraries & version control of references
q: Why put references under version control when the tool already syncs?
a: Sync gives you the current state; version control gives you history, blame and review. When a reviewer asks why a year changed, `git log -p refs/handbook.bib` answers in seconds, whereas a synced library shows only the latest values. It also decouples the manuscript from any one vendor: a `.bib` file in the repository builds with Pandoc or LaTeX regardless of whether Zotero or EndNote exists tomorrow. The cost is a small setup and the discipline of committing, which is why I automate the export.

chapter: Collaborative libraries & version control of references
q: What breaks when someone shares an EndNote library through Dropbox?
a: EndNote writes constantly to the `.Data` folder's index files, and sync engines upload partially written files or create "conflicted copy" duplicates, which corrupts the index and can corrupt the `.enl`. Two users opening it simultaneously makes it worse. The symptoms are missing references, a library that opens as empty, or "library is damaged" prompts. The remedy is Tools → Recover Library on a copy, then moving to EndNote's own sharing, and I mention that Clarivate's documentation explicitly warns against cloud-folder sharing.

chapter: QA checklist for reference lists (100+ entries)
q: How do you know a 400-entry reference list is correct before delivery?
a: I run a staged checklist and produce a report with counts. Structural checks first: citation-to-list matching from the plugin or a script, duplicates, order, field errors. Then field-level checks: every DOI resolved and compared against Crossref metadata for year, pages and title, author lists per the style's rule, consistent journal names, title case. Then typographic checks with Find: hanging indent by style, en dashes, italics. Finally a sample read of every tenth entry against the style's examples and a full read of narrative citations. The report lists what passed, what I fixed, and what remains open for the client, such as entries with no DOI or uncited works.

chapter: QA checklist for reference lists (100+ entries)
q: What are the most common errors you find in lists that look fine at a glance?
a: Year mismatches between text and list, where the text says 2019 and the list 2020 because the client cited an online-first version; page ranges truncated or hyphenated; DOIs with a single wrong character; two entries for the same paper differing only by a subtitle; and author lists cut at seven by an APA 6 import. None of these are visible without checking against a registry or matching the two halves, which is why I automate those two steps first.

chapter: QA checklist for reference lists (100+ entries)
q: A client disputes the hours for reference QA. How do you justify them?
a: With the report: 412 entries, 386 DOIs resolved, 7 Crossref mismatches corrected, 41 duplicates merged, 3 open items, each with the method used. I keep the checklist as a template so the numbers are consistent across projects, and I quote QA as a separate line so the client sees it as a deliverable rather than overhead. In practice the report also protects the client, because an examiner or copy-editor asking about a specific entry can be answered from it.

q: Tell me about your process when a client sends a document and says "fix the references".
a: I start with a diagnosis, not formatting: Alt+F9 to see whether citations are fields or text, a count of citations and entries, a check of which style is required and whether a written guide exists, and a citation-to-list match to find orphans. That gives me a scoped estimate with a rebuild component if the citations are text. Then the library is built by identifier, cleaned, the document formatted once, QA'd against my checklist, and delivered as a fields copy, a plain copy, the library export and a short report with counts. The report is what clients remember and what brings repeat work.

q: What would you do in your first week in a publications team that has no reference standard?
a: Audit what exists: which styles the last ten documents used, which tools people have, and where sources are stored. Propose one shared library, usually a Zotero group because it is free and cross-platform unless EndNote licences exist, one house style as a CSL file under version control, and a two-page SOP covering add-by-identifier, cite-from-group and the QA checklist. Then run one live document through it end to end with the team so the process is demonstrated rather than described.

q: How do you handle a disagreement with an author who insists their reference formatting is correct?
a: I point to the guide, not to my opinion: the specific page of the APA manual or the university's Harvard guide and the example for that source type. If the guide is ambiguous, which happens with Harvard, I document the choice and apply it consistently, because consistency is what examiners and copy-editors actually check. If the author's version contradicts the guide, I show the two side by side and let them decide with the consequence stated. The reference list belongs to the author; my job is to make sure it is defensible.

q: Which mistakes would make you reject a candidate for a formatting role?
a: Editing rendered citation text by hand, because it shows they do not understand fields; not knowing that APA 7 uses et al. from the first citation, because that is the commonest correction in current work; sharing an EndNote library through a sync folder; and delivering without any check that every citation has an entry. Each of these produces a document that looks finished and fails review. Conversely, a candidate who asks "which Harvard?" or "footnotes or author-date?" before starting has shown the judgement the role needs.

chapter: Introduction & three ways to add CSS
q: What are the three ways to add CSS and when is each appropriate?
a: External stylesheets linked from the head are the default: reusable across pages, cacheable and easy to maintain. Internal `<style>` blocks suit single-file outputs such as a WeasyPrint report template, an email-attached HTML file or a prototype. Inline `style` attributes should be reserved for HTML email, where clients strip stylesheets, and for values computed per element from data, like chart bar widths. The trade-off is reuse and caching versus self-containment and precedence; a strong answer notes that inline styles are also a maintenance and CSP problem, since a strict `style-src` policy blocks them.

chapter: Introduction & three ways to add CSS
q: Why does "separation of concerns" matter between HTML and CSS?
a: HTML carries structure and meaning that screen readers, search engines, PDF engines and e-readers depend on; CSS carries presentation, which differs per medium. Keeping them apart lets one HTML document render as a website, an A4 PDF and a reflowable EPUB by swapping stylesheets, which is exactly how my report pipeline works. It also means a redesign touches CSS only, and content authors cannot break the layout. The exception that proves the rule is HTML email, where the lack of stylesheet support forces presentation back into the markup.

chapter: Introduction & three ways to add CSS
q: What is the CSSOM?
a: The CSS Object Model is the tree of parsed stylesheets and rules that the browser builds alongside the DOM, and the API JavaScript uses to read and change styles (`document.styleSheets`, `getComputedStyle`, `element.style`). Rendering needs both trees: the browser matches CSSOM rules against DOM elements to compute styles, then lays out and paints. Because the CSSOM must be complete before rendering, stylesheets are render-blocking, which is why they belong in the head and why large stylesheets delay first paint.

q: How does the browser match selectors, and why does it matter?
a: Browsers match selectors right to left: for `nav ul li a`, they first find every `a`, then check whether each has an `li` ancestor, then a `ul`, then a `nav`. This means the rightmost part (the key selector) determines how much work is done; `.sidebar *` or `div span` are expensive because the key is broad. In practice, selector performance rarely matters on modern engines except for very large DOMs, but the same reasoning explains why short, class-based selectors are easier to read and override. Interviewers want the right-to-left fact and a sensible "it usually does not matter" caveat.

q: When should you use an id selector versus a class?
a: Almost never for styling. Ids are unique, so they cannot be reused, and their specificity (1,0,0) overpowers any number of classes, which makes later overrides painful and pushes teams toward `!important`. Classes compose, repeat and are easy to override in order. Ids stay valuable for fragment links, `<label for>`, ARIA relationships and `getElementById`. If I need to target a unique element in CSS I still give it a class, or use `[id="summary"]`, which has class-level specificity.

q: What is the difference between `ul li` and `ul > li` in a nested list?
a: `ul li` matches every `li` that has any `ul` ancestor, so in a two-level list it matches both levels; `ul > li` matches only `li` elements whose direct parent is a `ul`, but since nested `li` elements also have a `ul` parent, it still matches both levels! To target only the top level you scope from a known ancestor, such as `nav > ul > li`, or exclude the nested ones with `li:not(li li)`. This trick question checks whether the candidate actually thinks about the tree rather than reciting definitions.

q: When would you use HSL instead of hex?
a: Hex is what brand guides and design tools hand you, so it is the source of truth for fixed colours. HSL shines when colours are derived: hover and active states by lowering lightness, tints for table stripes by raising it, and whole palettes by rotating hue with the same saturation and lightness so they feel related. It is also readable: `hsl(205 79% 40%)` tells me "a medium, saturated blue" while `#1572B6` tells me nothing. The trade-off is that HSL lightness is not perceptually uniform, so yellow at 50% looks far brighter than blue at 50%; `oklch()` fixes that in modern browsers, though WeasyPrint's support for new colour spaces lags.

q: How do you ensure colour accessibility in a report or dashboard?
a: Check every text/background pair against WCAG AA ratios, 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and UI borders, using DevTools or a contrast checker, and fix by darkening text rather than lightening backgrounds. Never rely on colour alone for meaning: pair status colours with text or icons, and use patterns or labels in charts for colour-blind readers, roughly 8% of men. Keep the palette small and consistent so meaning is learnable. For print I also test in greyscale, since many clients print dashboards on monochrome office printers.

q: Why might a background colour disappear when a page is printed?
a: Browsers default to not printing backgrounds to save ink, controlled by the user's "Background graphics" checkbox; `print-color-adjust: exact` on the element asks the browser to keep them, and a print stylesheet can also swap backgrounds for borders. WeasyPrint prints backgrounds unconditionally, so a template that looks right in WeasyPrint may still print blank cells from a browser. For table headers I set both a background and a bottom border so the structure survives either way.

q: How does `@font-face` work and what are the pitfalls?
a: `@font-face` maps a family name plus weight and style to a font file, so later `font-family` references can use it like an installed font. Pitfalls: every weight and style needs its own declaration or the browser synthesises fake bold and italic; the file must be served with CORS headers if it lives on another origin; licences differ between web use and PDF/EPUB embedding; large files delay text rendering, which `font-display: swap` and subsetting with `pyftsubset` address; and PDF engines like WeasyPrint need TTF/OTF/WOFF files reachable from the HTML's `base_url`, never a Google Fonts link. I keep a per-client `fonts/` folder with the licence file next to the WOFF2 and TTF versions.

q: What is the difference between `em` and `rem` for font sizes?
a: `rem` is relative to the root (`html`) font size, so `1.25rem` is the same everywhere; `em` is relative to the current element's inherited font size, so nested `em` values compound (a `1.2em` list inside a `1.2em` section becomes 1.44×). Use `rem` for font sizes and spacing that should be consistent, and `em` for values that should scale with the element's own text, such as `letter-spacing`, `padding` on a button or an icon's size. In EPUB I use `em` throughout because readers change the base size and everything should follow proportionally.

q: Why does justified text look bad on the web but good in books?
a: Books justify with hyphenation, careful word spacing and a measure of 60–70 characters, so the "rivers" of white space stay small. Browsers historically had no hyphenation and pages have unpredictable widths, so justification produced ugly gaps, especially on narrow phones. Today `hyphens: auto` with a correct `lang` attribute, a limited measure (`max-width: 65ch`) and `text-wrap: pretty` in newer Chrome make justified web text acceptable. WeasyPrint hyphenates with language dictionaries, so for PDF handbooks I justify with hyphens on and keep it left-aligned for screens.

q: Explain the CSS box model and the difference between `content-box` and `border-box`.
a: Every element generates a box with content, padding, border and margin layers. With the default `content-box`, `width` and `height` size only the content, so padding and border add to the rendered size; with `border-box`, they size the border edge, so padding and border fit inside. `border-box` makes percentage layouts predictable and matches how designers think, which is why the universal reset `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box }` is standard. Margins are never included in either model. A complete answer also mentions margin collapsing between vertical block margins and that `outline` sits outside the box without affecting layout.

q: When would you use `em`, `rem`, `%`, `vw` and `px`?
a: `rem` for font sizes and a spacing scale, so everything follows the root size and user zoom; `em` for properties that should scale with the element's own text, such as button padding and letter-spacing; `%` for widths relative to a parent in fluid layouts; `vw`/`vh` for viewport-relative sizing such as hero sections or fluid type inside `clamp()`; and `px` for hairline borders, shadows and other details that should not scale. In print CSS I switch to `pt` and `mm` because output is physical. The key point is choosing the reference each value should track, not memorising rules.

q: What is margin collapsing and when does it not happen?
a: When two vertical margins touch, between siblings or between a parent and its first or last child, they combine into a single margin equal to the larger one rather than adding. It exists so that paragraph spacing stays even regardless of nesting. Collapsing does not happen horizontally, across padding or borders, inside flex or grid containers, for floated or absolutely positioned elements, or when a new block formatting context is created (`display: flow-root`, `overflow: hidden`). The classic bug is a child's top margin pushing its parent down; adding `padding-top: 1px` or `display: flow-root` to the parent fixes it.

q: Explain the difference between `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed` and `sticky`.
a: `relative` keeps the element in normal flow, preserves its original space and offsets the painted box; its most important side effect is becoming the containing block for absolutely positioned descendants. `absolute` removes the element from flow and positions it against the nearest positioned ancestor. `fixed` is the same idea but against the viewport, so it does not move on scroll, unless an ancestor has a `transform`, which then becomes the containing block. `sticky` stays in flow and toggles to fixed-like behaviour when its scroll offset is reached, but only within its parent's bounds and only if no ancestor clips overflow. In a report viewer I use sticky for table headers, absolute for badges inside cards, and fixed for a "back to top" control.

q: What is a stacking context and why does a huge `z-index` sometimes not work?
a: A stacking context is a self-contained layer group; elements inside it are ordered among themselves, then the whole context is placed as one unit in its parent context. Contexts are created by the root, by positioned elements with a `z-index`, by `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, `isolation: isolate` and a few others. A child cannot escape its context, so a menu with `z-index: 9999` inside a header with `z-index: 1` still sits behind a sibling with `z-index: 2`. The fix is to identify the ancestor creating the context with DevTools' Layers panel and either raise that ancestor or restructure the DOM so the overlay is a sibling of the content, which is why modals are usually appended to `body`.

q: What does `display: flow-root` do and when would you use it?
a: It makes the element a block that establishes a new block formatting context. Practically that means it contains its floated children, so the parent no longer collapses to zero height, and it prevents its children's margins from collapsing through it. It replaces the old clearfix hack (`::after { content: ""; display: table; clear: both }`) and is cleaner than `overflow: hidden`, which also clips shadows and tooltips. I use it on article wrappers that contain floated figures and on card bodies where a first-child heading's margin was escaping the card.

q: When would you choose Flexbox over Grid?
a: Flexbox distributes items along one axis and lets content size decide the layout, so it fits toolbars, navigation, button groups, tag lists and vertical stacks where items should size to their content and wrap naturally. Grid places items in two dimensions against explicit tracks, so it fits page scaffolds, dashboards and forms where columns must align across rows. A practical rule is content-out versus layout-in: if I am asking "spread these things out", Flexbox; if I am asking "put this in row 2, columns 1 to 3", Grid. They nest well, and a typical page is a Grid shell with Flexbox components inside.

q: Explain `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink` and `flex-basis` with an example.
a: `flex-basis` is the item's starting size on the main axis, `flex-grow` is its share of any leftover space, and `flex-shrink` its share of any deficit, both weighted relative to siblings. For a sidebar layout, `.sidebar { flex: 0 0 240px }` never grows or shrinks and starts at 240px, while `.main { flex: 1 1 0 }` starts from zero and takes all remaining space. If two items have `flex-grow: 1` and `2`, the second gets twice as much of the extra space, not twice the width. Shrinking is additionally weighted by basis size, which is why a long item shrinks more than a short one with the same `flex-shrink`.

q: Why does a flex item sometimes refuse to shrink and overflow its container?
a: Because the default `min-width` for flex items is `auto`, which resolves to the item's minimum content size; a long unbroken URL or a wide table sets a floor the item will not go below, so it overflows. Setting `min-width: 0` (or `overflow: hidden`) on the item lets it shrink, after which `overflow-x: auto` or `overflow-wrap: anywhere` inside it handles the content. The same applies to `min-height: auto` in column direction. It is one of the most searched CSS bugs and a good candidate explains both the cause and the fix.

q: What is the difference between `auto-fill` and `auto-fit`?
a: Both create as many columns as fit the container using the `minmax()` size you give them. `auto-fill` keeps any empty tracks, so with three cards in a row that could hold five you get three cards and two blank slots, which keeps card widths stable. `auto-fit` collapses the empty tracks to zero, so the three cards stretch to fill the row. I use `auto-fit` for card grids that should always look full, and `auto-fill` when consistent item width matters, such as a form where a lone field should not become enormously wide.

q: How do implicit and explicit grids differ?
a: The explicit grid is what you declare with `grid-template-columns`, `grid-template-rows` and `grid-template-areas`. When items are auto-placed beyond it, or placed at a line that does not exist, the browser creates implicit tracks, sized by `grid-auto-rows` and `grid-auto-columns` (default `auto`). `grid-auto-flow` controls placement direction and `dense` packing. A typical bug is defining two rows, adding a fifth item, and wondering why the third row has no height: it is implicit and needs `grid-auto-rows`.

q: How would you build a responsive layout with Grid without media queries?
a: Use intrinsic sizing: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 240px), 1fr))` makes columns that are at least 240px, collapse to a single column when the container is narrower, and never overflow thanks to `min(100%, 240px)`. Combine it with `gap` and `fr` units, and with container queries for component-level changes, and most dashboards never need a viewport breakpoint. Named areas with a media query are still simpler for page-level reflows such as moving navigation below content, so I use both: intrinsic grids for components, one or two queries for the shell.

q: What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
a: A pseudo-class selects existing elements based on a state or position the markup does not express, such as `:hover`, `:checked`, `:nth-child(odd)` or `:has(img)`; it uses one colon and adds specificity like a class. A pseudo-element addresses a part of an element or a generated box, such as `::before`, `::first-line` or `::placeholder`; it uses two colons and counts like a tag in specificity. Only one pseudo-element may appear per selector and it must be last. A typical use combining both is `li:not(:last-child)::after { content: "," }` to render a comma-separated list from plain markup.

q: How do `:is()`, `:where()` and `:has()` change how you write CSS?
a: `:is()` shortens selector lists (`:is(h1, h2, h3) a` instead of three rules) and takes the specificity of its most specific argument. `:where()` is identical but contributes zero specificity, which makes it ideal for resets and framework defaults that authors should override with a single class. `:has()` is the parent and sibling selector CSS never had: `label:has(+ input:invalid)` or `.card:has(> img)` change styling based on descendants, replacing JavaScript class toggling for many cases. The cost of `:has()` is that the browser must re-evaluate it when descendants change, so avoid `:has()` with deep unbounded descendant selectors on large DOMs.

q: How do CSS counters work and where have you used them?
a: `counter-reset: name` creates a counter on an element, `counter-increment: name` bumps it on each matching element, and `counter(name)` or `counters(name, ".")` prints it inside `content`. Nested counters give "2.3.1" outline numbering when you reset the child counter on each parent. I use them for heading numbers, figure and table captions, and page numbers in print stylesheets with `content: counter(page) " of " counter(pages)`, which WeasyPrint supports. They keep numbering correct when sections are reordered, which was a constant source of errors in hand-numbered Word manuals.

q: Walk me through how the browser decides which declaration wins.
a: For each property on each element it gathers every matching declaration, then filters in a fixed order: origin and importance first (normal author beats user beats user-agent, and `!important` reverses that), then cascade layers (later layer wins, unlayered author styles beat all layers), then specificity as an (ID, class, type) triple compared left to right, then source order, where the last declaration wins. Inline styles act as if they had specificity above any selector, and `!important` beats inline. Only after the cascade does inheritance fill in properties that no rule set, using the parent's computed value for inherited properties or the initial value otherwise. Being able to say this in order, and to name `@layer`, is what distinguishes a current answer from a 2015 one.

q: Why are IDs and `!important` discouraged in selectors?
a: Both break the escalation ladder. An ID selector can only be overridden by another ID or `!important`, so a component styled with `#header a` forces every theme to repeat the ID; `!important` can only be beaten by another `!important` later in source, so once one appears they multiply. Low, flat specificity, one class per rule with `:where()` for defaults, keeps overrides predictable: a later class wins. Cascade layers solve the same problem structurally, letting a utilities layer beat components without any specificity contest. I keep `!important` for utility classes and print overrides where "always" is genuinely the intent.

q: What is the difference between `initial`, `inherit`, `unset` and `revert`?
a: `inherit` copies the parent's computed value even for non-inherited properties like `border`. `initial` sets the specification's initial value, which is frequently surprising: `display: initial` is `inline` and `color: initial` is black regardless of the UA stylesheet. `unset` behaves as `inherit` for inherited properties and `initial` for the rest, so it is what `all: unset` uses to strip an element. `revert` rolls back to the value the previous origin would have given, so `display: revert` on a `div` is `block`, making it the right choice for "undo my styling but keep browser defaults", and `revert-layer` does the same one cascade layer up.

q: What is mobile-first design and why is it the default recommendation?
a: Mobile-first means the base stylesheet, with no media queries, targets the smallest screen, and `min-width` queries progressively add layout as room appears. It forces content priority decisions early, produces smaller CSS for phones because they skip the queries entirely, and matches how CSS naturally works: a single-column stack is the default flow, so you add complexity rather than undoing it. Desktop-first with `max-width` queries tends to accumulate overrides that reset floats, widths and grids. The exception is a genuinely desktop-only internal tool, where the extra work has no audience.

q: How do container queries differ from media queries and when do you use each?
a: Media queries test the viewport (or print) and are right for page-level decisions such as the number of layout columns or hiding a sidebar. Container queries test the size of a declared ancestor with `container-type`, so a component can adapt to where it is placed: the same KPI card renders stacked in a 240px sidebar and side-by-side in the main column on the same screen. They make components portable between pages and design systems, which media queries cannot because the component does not know its context. The rule I follow is shell decisions in media queries, component decisions in container queries, and fluid techniques like `clamp()` and `auto-fit` grids before either.

q: How do you keep a wide data table usable on phones?
a: First accept that tables cannot reflow below their content, so wrap them in `overflow-x: auto` with `-webkit-overflow-scrolling` no longer needed, and make the first column sticky so row labels stay visible. Reduce padding and font size slightly, hide low-priority columns with a `max-width` query, and consider a "cards" transformation where each row becomes a block with `td::before { content: attr(data-label) }` supplying the column name. For very long reports, offer a download or a landscape print stylesheet rather than fighting the viewport. I have shipped all of these for rate matrices with fifteen columns.

q: What is the difference between a transition and an animation?
a: A transition interpolates a property between its old and new value when something changes it, such as a class toggle or `:hover`; it has one implicit start and end and cannot loop or define intermediate steps. An animation is defined by `@keyframes` with any number of steps, runs as soon as it is applied, can repeat, alternate and pause, and does not need a state change to start. Use transitions for interactive feedback and animations for attention, loading and entrance effects. Both fire DOM events (`transitionend`, `animationend`) and both are cancelled if the element is removed or `display: none` is applied.

q: Why are `transform` and `opacity` recommended for animation, and what is `will-change`?
a: The rendering pipeline is style, layout, paint and composite. Changing geometry properties such as `width` or `top` forces layout of the element and possibly its neighbours on every frame; changing `background` forces repaint. `transform` and `opacity` can be applied by the compositor to an already-painted layer, so a 60fps animation costs almost nothing on the main thread. `will-change: transform` hints the browser to promote the element to its own layer in advance so the first frame does not stutter, but each layer costs GPU memory, so apply it just before the animation and remove it after, or only to a handful of elements.

q: How would you animate an accordion whose content height is unknown?
a: `height: auto` cannot be transitioned in most browsers. The robust CSS-only approach is a grid wrapper: `grid-template-rows: 0fr` closed and `1fr` open, with the inner element set to `overflow: hidden`, and `fr` values interpolate smoothly. Alternatives are `max-height` with a generous cap (easing looks wrong because the interpolation runs to the cap), measuring `scrollHeight` in JavaScript and setting an explicit height, or `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` in Chromium 129+. I choose the grid method by default because it needs no measurement and survives content changes.

q: How do CSS custom properties differ from Sass variables?
a: Sass variables are resolved at compile time into literal values and disappear from the output, so they cannot respond to the viewport, a theme class, a component's ancestor or JavaScript. Custom properties are real cascaded, inherited values evaluated in the browser: `--accent` set on `.card.warning` re-colours every descendant rule, a media query can redefine tokens for dark mode, and `element.style.setProperty` updates them live. Sass still wins for things CSS cannot do at runtime, such as breakpoints, loops and mixins, so many teams use Sass for structure and custom properties for tokens and theming.

q: What does "invalid at computed-value time" mean and how do you guard against it?
a: When a `var()` substitution produces a value the property cannot parse, the browser has already discarded other declarations for that property during cascade, so it cannot fall back to an earlier rule; the property becomes `unset`, which is `inherit` for inherited properties and `initial` otherwise. That can silently drop a width or turn text the parent's colour. Guards are a fallback in `var(--x, 16px)`, always defining tokens on `:root`, and registering the property with `@property` and an `initial-value`, which also gives typed interpolation. Linting with Stylelint's `custom-property-no-missing-var-function` and a token file that is the single source of truth catch most mistakes.

q: Give an example where `calc()` with a custom property removed JavaScript from a project.
a: A progress bar and a chart with bars sized from data: the server renders `style="--pct: 72%"` on each row and CSS does `width: var(--pct)`, with `@property` making the value animate on update. Another is a sidebar layout where `--sidebar: 240px` drives both the sidebar width and `calc(100% - var(--sidebar))` for the main column, so collapsing the sidebar is a single variable change on a class rather than resizing two elements in script. In a WeasyPrint report I also used `calc()` to compute column widths from a `--cols` variable so one stylesheet served five-column and seven-column rate matrices.

q: How do you load a brand web font without hurting performance or layout stability?
a: Convert to WOFF2, subset it to the scripts actually used, and declare one `@font-face` per weight with `font-display: swap` so text is never invisible. Preload the body regular weight with `<link rel="preload" as="font" crossorigin>` so it starts downloading before CSS is parsed, and self-host rather than using a third-party CDN to avoid an extra connection. To limit layout shift, choose a fallback with similar metrics and tune it with `size-adjust`, `ascent-override` and `descent-override` in a second `@font-face` for the fallback family. Measure with Lighthouse's CLS and the font-display audit, and prefer a variable font when three or more weights are needed.

q: What makes a good typographic scale and how do you implement it?
a: A scale is a small set of sizes related by a consistent ratio (1.2 to 1.333 for text-heavy sites, larger for marketing) so heading hierarchy is visible without being arbitrary. Implement it as custom properties (`--fs-0` to `--fs-4`) computed from a base, wrap the large steps in `clamp()` so they scale fluidly with the viewport, and pair each step with an appropriate line-height, tight for display sizes and 1.5 for body. Spacing then follows the same rhythm, using multiples of the body line-height for margins. Tools like Utopia generate the clamp values; the important part is that every element references a token rather than a literal size.

q: How does typography differ between web, PDF and EPUB outputs of the same document?
a: On the web I use `rem` sizes, fluid `clamp()` headings, `max-width: 65ch` and `text-wrap: pretty`. For print via WeasyPrint I switch to points and millimetres, enable `hyphens: auto` with `text-align: justify`, set `orphans: 2; widows: 2`, and embed fonts by file path since there is no network. For EPUB I keep sizes in `em` relative to the reader's chosen base, avoid fixed line-height and `!important` so user settings win, keep font stacks simple because embedded fonts are optional on most readers, and never rely on `ch` or `clamp()` for older devices. The shared part is the token names and hierarchy; only the values and units change per target.

q: How do you make a wide data table work on a phone without losing information?
a: The first option is a scroll wrapper with `overflow-x: auto` and a sticky first column, which keeps the table semantics and works for any column count. The second is the stacked pattern: under a `max-width` query, hide `thead`, display each row as a block and each cell as a flex row with `td::before { content: attr(data-label) }` supplying the header text, which reads naturally on a narrow screen but needs the `data-label` attributes generated in the template. I choose scrolling for numeric matrices where comparing columns matters and stacking for record-style tables such as a list of files with a few fields each. In both cases `table-layout: fixed` and `overflow-wrap: anywhere` prevent a single long value from breaking the layout.

q: What are the accessibility essentials of a styled form?
a: Every control has a programmatically associated label (`<label for>` or wrapping), placeholders are hints not labels, and hints and errors are linked with `aria-describedby`. Focus is always visible with a `:focus-visible` style of at least 3:1 contrast, and hover effects do not replace it. Validation states use text or icons in addition to colour, errors appear near the field and are announced, and required fields are marked in text, not only with an asterisk colour. Controls have at least 24 by 24 CSS pixel targets, `font-size` of 1rem to avoid iOS zoom, and native semantics are kept where possible (`accent-color` instead of rebuilding checkboxes) so keyboard and screen-reader behaviour comes for free.

q: `table-layout: auto` versus `fixed`: what changes?
a: With `auto`, the browser reads every cell to compute column widths, so the widest content wins and rendering a 5,000-row table waits on the whole table. With `fixed`, widths come from the table's width plus the first row or `<col>` elements, the browser can render rows as they arrive, and long content wraps or overflows within its column rather than resizing it. `fixed` is faster and predictable and is what I use for rate matrices and reports; `auto` is better for small tables whose content varies wildly. `fixed` requires an explicit `width` on the table, otherwise it behaves like `auto`.

q: How do you produce automatic page numbers, running headers and a TOC from HTML?
a: With a paged-media engine such as WeasyPrint, Prince or Paged.js, the `@page` rule defines size and margins and its margin boxes (`@top-left`, `@bottom-center` and so on) hold generated content. `counter(page)` and `counter(pages)` give "Page X of Y"; `string-set: chapter content()` on `h1` plus `content: string(chapter)` in a margin box gives a running header that changes per chapter, and `position: running()` with `element()` does the same with rich HTML. A TOC is a list of links whose `::after` prints `target-counter(attr(href), page)` with `leader(".")` for dots. Breaks are controlled with `break-before: page` on chapters, `break-after: avoid` on headings and `break-inside: avoid` on figures and rows. Browsers only implement a subset (page size, margins, breaks), so the full stack needs the dedicated engine.

q: What are the main differences between browser print and WeasyPrint, and how do you develop for both?
a: Browsers support `@page size` and margins, `break-*`, `orphans`/`widows` and repeat `thead`, but not margin boxes, `string-set`, `target-counter`, `leader()` or PDF bookmarks, and Chrome's `counter(pages)` is missing. WeasyPrint supports all of those but runs no JavaScript, has partial support for some newer layout features depending on version, and loads fonts and images from file paths. I develop the layout in the browser with `@media print` and DevTools' print emulation for fast iteration, then add a `print.css` layer with the paged-media features and check the PDF in WeasyPrint with `--debug` logging for unsupported declarations. Keeping content and structure in HTML and pagination in CSS means the same source also renders as a web page and an EPUB.

q: A 700-page PDF from WeasyPrint takes too long or too much memory. What do you do?
a: First profile: WeasyPrint's cost is dominated by layout of huge tables and by images, so split enormous tables into per-page chunks or use `table-layout: fixed`, downscale images to the print resolution (300 dpi at final size, not 4000px originals), and convert PNG screenshots to JPEG where transparency is not needed. Avoid `break-inside: avoid` on large blocks because the engine retries layout, and remove unused `@font-face` declarations. Render chapters as separate PDFs in parallel and merge with pikepdf or pypdf, then rebuild bookmarks, which also lets a change in one chapter re-render only that chapter. Finally, keep WeasyPrint current: versions 60 and later are substantially faster than 52, and its image optimisation options shrink output.

chapter: CSS for EPUB (reflowable vs fixed layout)
q: How does EPUB CSS differ from website CSS?
a: The renderer is not one browser but a dozen reading systems with partial CSS support and a user stylesheet that must win, so EPUB CSS is deliberately minimal and defensive: `em` units, no body font size or colour, legacy and modern break properties side by side, no Flexbox or Grid for essential layout, no `!important`, images capped at 100% width, and fonts embedded but never required. EPUB also has features the web lacks or rarely uses: `epub:type` semantics for pop-up footnotes, vendor media queries such as `amzn-kf8`, the `rendition:` properties for fixed layout and spreads, and a required navigation document. The test matrix is Thorium, Apple Books, Kobo, ADE and Kindle Previewer plus `epubcheck`, not Chrome and Firefox.

chapter: CSS for EPUB (reflowable vs fixed layout)
q: When would you choose fixed layout, and what does it cost?
a: Fixed layout is right when the page design is the content: children's picture books, comics, illustrated cookbooks, brochures and magazines where text must sit at a precise spot over an image. It costs reflow and accessibility: fonts cannot be enlarged, phones show tiny pages, screen readers get a worse experience, and the file is much larger. Distributors also limit it; Kindle wants a special KF8 fixed-layout package and Kobo's FXL support is uneven. For a client's illustrated brochure I produce FXL with selectable text over an SVG background and, where feasible, a reflowable companion edition for accessibility.

chapter: CSS for EPUB (reflowable vs fixed layout)
q: How do you handle fonts and colours so a book works in night mode and with user settings?
a: I leave `color` and `background` off `body` and paragraphs entirely so the reader's theme provides both, and use borders rather than fills for callouts, with any decorative colours chosen to be legible on both white and black. Font sizes are `em` relative to the reader's base; line-height is unitless; headings may use an embedded display face declared with `@font-face` but with a generic fallback and no `!important`. Images with transparent backgrounds and dark line art get a light backing colour or are exported as JPEG with white, because transparent PNGs on a black night-mode page vanish. Then I test in Apple Books night mode, Kobo's dark theme and Thorium's sepia to confirm nothing disappears.

q: Compare BEM and utility-first CSS. Which would you choose for a new project?
a: BEM gives every component an explicit, greppable name with flat one-class specificity, and the HTML stays readable, but you spend effort naming and you accumulate dead rules unless disciplined. Utility-first removes naming and dead CSS, enforces the design tokens because only token-valued classes exist, and keeps changes local to the template, at the cost of long class lists and repetition unless you have a component layer in the templating system. For a design-system-driven app with React or Jinja components I would go utility-first with extracted components; for a content site, a WeasyPrint report or an EPUB, where the HTML is the deliverable and must stay clean, I would use BEM-style component classes with a handful of utilities. In either case cascade layers and a linter enforcing no IDs and low specificity do more for maintainability than the naming scheme.

q: How do you prevent specificity wars in a large codebase?
a: Keep specificity flat and rising only with intent: single-class selectors for components, `:where()` for element defaults so any class overrides them, no IDs in selectors, no `!important` outside utilities, and `@layer` to express precedence structurally (reset, base, components, utilities) so a utility beats a component without escalation. Vendor CSS goes in its own low layer via `@import … layer()`. Stylelint enforces the rules on every pull request. When an override is still needed, add a modifier class rather than a longer selector, and if two rules with the same specificity conflict, source order in a defined file sequence decides, which is documented rather than accidental.

q: What are cascade layers and how would you migrate an existing stylesheet to them?
a: `@layer` groups rules into named layers with a declared order; a later layer always beats an earlier one for normal declarations regardless of selector specificity, and unlayered styles beat all layers. To migrate, first declare the order at the top (`@layer reset, vendor, base, components, utilities`), then move third-party imports into `layer(vendor)` since they are the most common override problem, then wrap your reset and base. Existing component CSS can stay unlayered temporarily because unlayered styles have top priority, which means nothing visibly changes; finally move components and utilities into their layers and delete the `!important`s that were only there to beat the vendor styles. `revert-layer` helps when a component needs to fall back to base styling inside a layer.

q: Explain the browser's critical rendering path and where CSS sits in it.
a: The browser parses HTML into the DOM, discovers stylesheets and parses them into the CSSOM, combines the two into a render tree of visible elements with computed styles, lays out geometry, paints layers and composites them. CSS is render-blocking: nothing paints until every stylesheet in `<head>` that matches the current media has arrived, and scripts that read styles wait for the CSSOM too. So the levers are fewer and smaller stylesheets, no `@import` chains, `media` attributes to unblock non-matching sheets, preloading late-discovered CSS and fonts, and inlining a small critical subset when first paint is the priority. After load, the same pipeline runs on every change, so the second concern is which stage a property change invalidates.

q: How would you diagnose a page that scrolls or animates at 20 fps?
a: Record with the Performance panel while reproducing, and look for long frames: purple bars are layout and style recalculation, green are paint. If style recalculation dominates, find the class toggle or `:has()`/universal selector on a large subtree and narrow it, or use `contain`. If layout dominates, look for animated geometry properties or JavaScript that reads layout inside a write loop (layout thrashing), and switch to `transform`, batch reads with writes, or apply `content-visibility: auto` to long lists. If paint dominates, enable Paint flashing and look for large repainting areas from `box-shadow`, `backdrop-filter` or a fixed background, then isolate the animated element on its own layer with `will-change` for the duration of the animation. Verify on a throttled mobile profile and compare frame times before and after.

q: What is CLS and how do CSS decisions cause or prevent it?
a: Cumulative Layout Shift measures how much visible content moves without user interaction. CSS causes it when space is not reserved: images and iframes without `width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio`, web fonts that swap in with different metrics, ads or banners injected at the top, and animating properties like `height` or `top` on elements that push neighbours. Prevention is reserving space with intrinsic dimensions and `aspect-ratio`, matching fallback font metrics with `size-adjust` and `ascent-override`, using `font-display: optional` where a font swap is worse than a system font, `min-height` on containers whose content arrives later, and animating only `transform` and `opacity`. In a client's dashboard, adding `aspect-ratio` on chart containers took CLS from 0.31 to under 0.05.

q: You are handed a broken layout with no context. How do you approach it?
a: Open DevTools and inspect the misbehaving element, checking the computed box (size, padding, margins) and the crossed-out declarations to see which rules lost the cascade and why. Then identify which formatting context it lives in: is the parent a flex or grid container, is anything positioned, is there a stacking context or an `overflow` clip above it, and what is the containing block?
